name: How do I know if my pool needs full removal instead of a fill-in?

mainEntity.name: What signs suggest that a partial removal is not enough and the pool should be fully demolished?
mainEntity.text: What signs suggest that a partial removal is not enough and the pool should be fully demolished?

acceptedAnswer.text: Partial fill-ins are often used when the goal is simply to remove an unwanted pool at the lowest cost. Full removal becomes more attractive when future construction, major landscaping, or resale flexibility matters. If the pool shell is heavily damaged, the site has drainage problems, or the yard may later support an addition, garage, ADU, or large hardscape area, removing the entire shell can reduce uncertainty. Full removal also gives contractors a cleaner subgrade for future work. Homeowners should think about long-term plans, not just initial price. If there is any chance the space will be built over later, it is worth asking whether leaving buried shell material behind could complicate the next project.
acceptedAnswer.description: Full removal is often better when the property may be expanded, rebuilt, or heavily landscaped later. If the pool has major cracking, poor drainage, foundation concerns, or buried utilities in the work zone, full removal may be the safer long-term choice.
